entries.claim: On TACO, early and late frames of one take differ in contact amount about twice as much as two takes of the same mesh and verb at matched phase (time/take 2.12, above 1 in 8 of 8 groups), while their normalised spatial pattern differs about as much as between two such takes (time/take 1.04, above 1 in 3 of 8 groups); a different mesh at matched phase changes the pattern more than a different take does (mesh/take 1.48, 8 of 8 groups), and the within-take pattern change stays below the mesh-to-mesh difference in every group (time/mesh 0.69, 0 of 8 groups above 1).
entries.metric: Unitless ratio of two mean pair distances of the SAME metric inside one group (category x role x hand): numerator = pairs along one axis, denominator = pairs of two different takes of the same mesh and verb at matched phase (phase difference < 0.10). time = two frames of one take with phase difference > 0.5 (early vs late); mesh = other mesh, same verb, matched phase. amount = |difference of mass|, mass = sum of the 512-D soft contact map (soft = exp(-d / 2 cm)); pattern = L2 distance between maps normalised to sum 1 (defined only when neither frame is zero-contact). Headline = macro (unweighted mean of the 8 per-group ratios), mean over pairs. 1 = as different as two takes at the same phase; no direction is better. Experiment 1 of the dynamic-contact study; frames = every 2nd frame of 64-frame windows with touch fraction >= 0.2; up to 4000 cross pairs per group and axis, 3074-13369 time pairs per group.

caveats: The two ratios are in different metrics, each divided by its own cross-take level; '2.12 vs 1.04' is a comparison relative to take-to-take variation, not an absolute amount-versus-pattern comparison.

Pattern time/take is 1.036 as a macro mean but 0.964 pooled, and three of eight groups (spoon, roller, knife; all tool / right hand) are 1.3-1.5: say 'about the same as between two takes', not 'smaller than between takes'.
The macro values have no confidence interval in the sources; intervals exist per group only (95 % paired sequence-level bootstrap, 500 replicates).
'Mesh' on TACO is confounded with subject / session (report: tool meshes are used by 1-6 subjects, mean 2.1): the mesh ratio is 'the mesh and whoever used it', not pure geometry.

Phase is the position inside the touching span of a take, not an alignment of task events; 'time' means early vs late (phase difference > 0.5) inside takes of 64-448 windowed frames (median 128 = 4.3 s).
No grasp label exists in this study: the axes are take, mesh, action (verb); 'grasp identity' is not measured here.
Statement is about 512-D canonical contact maps only, not about hand motion.

entries.claim: On ARCTIC, where a take lasts 18-37 s, early and late frames of one take differ in normalised spatial pattern slightly less than two takes do (time/take 0.94, above 1 in 6 of 22 groups); in contact amount they differ about as much on |delta mass| (1.10, 14 of 22 groups) and more on log-mass (1.57, 22 of 22), and that excess is associated with pairs in which one frame is zero-contact (0.90 and 0.98 when neither frame is zero-contact); frames from a different subject differ in pattern 1.16 times the same-subject cross-take level (22 of 22 groups), which is 1.01 times the any-subject cross-take level that the time ratio uses (16 of 22 groups).

Takes are 512-1088 windowed frames (median 704 = 23.5 s) and contain several contact episodes; 17 % of frames are zero-contact. A phase gap of 0.5 is at least 10 s here against 1-2 s on TACO, so phase-based ratios are on a coarser time scale (report caveat).

Few within-take pairs: 473-612 time pairs per group (4000 for the cross axes), hence wide per-group intervals.
One mesh per object: nothing here tests geometry; the subject axis is confounded with session and hand size (report caveat).
The ARCTIC report states that on articulated objects amount and pattern grow together in the lag curves ('the location drifts with the amount'); the simple TACO picture is weakest here.
entries.claim_as_extracted: On ARCTIC, where a take lasts 18-37 s, early and late frames of one take differ in normalised spatial pattern slightly less than two takes do (time/take 0.94, above 1 in 6 of 22 groups) and in contact amount about as much (1.10 on |delta mass|, 14 of 22 groups; 1.57 on log-mass, 22 of 22), and that amount excess is associated with pairs in which one frame has no contact (0.90 and 0.98 once both frames are in contact); a different subject changes the pattern 1.16 times the same-subject cross-take level (22 of 22 groups).
entries.correction_reason: Every number is confirmed. Three wording fixes: 1.57 is not 'about as much'; 'in contact' should be 'neither frame zero-contact' (the both_nonzero variant; zero = mass < 4.0 and no vertex within 1 cm); and the subject ratio must carry its like-for-like value 1.011 in the same sentence, otherwise 1.16 is read against the 0.94 time ratio, which has a different denominator.

The last clause reads as an intervention on identical takes, but the two runs contain different take samples (1,985 against 3,239 takes in the 39 common groups, because the interaction-only index lost 1,780 rows without a frame count); state it as a comparison of two runs. entries.claim: On each of the three datasets the early-vs-late difference of the normalised spatial pattern within a take is near or below the take-to-take difference (time/take 1.04 on TACO, 0.94 on ARCTIC, 0.45 on OakInk2), and an identity axis exceeds its own cross-take reference (mesh/take 1.48 on TACO; object-instance/take 1.69 on OakInk2, over 17 of 39 groups; on ARCTIC subject over same-subject take 1.16, which is 1.01 against the any-subject take level used by the time ratio). The temporal excess of the amount differs by dataset in line with what a take contains (2.12 on TACO takes with approach and release, 1.10 on long multi-episode ARCTIC takes, 0.60 on interaction-only OakInk2 segments); the OakInk2 control run with approach and retreat included (1.38) is consistent with this reading.
entries.metric: Per dataset: macro mean over that dataset's groups of the ratio 'mean pair distance along an axis / mean matched-phase cross-take pair distance', same metric (amount = |delta mass|, pattern = L2 of the sum-normalised map). Values are reported per dataset and are never averaged across datasets. 1 = cross-take level; no direction is better.

caveats: The three identity ratios are not the same quantity: TACO and OakInk2 use mesh / take; ARCTIC uses subject / same-subject take (a different denominator); OakInk2 mesh/take covers 17 of 39 groups.

The amount ordering across datasets (2.12, 1.10, 0.60) follows how much approach, release and on/off each take contains, as the reports and the OakInk2 control state; it is not a statement about the datasets' objects.

The cross-dataset narrative's sentence 'whatever temporal excess exists is amount, not location' sits beside an ARCTIC report that marks the lag structure as a NOT-same conclusion (amount and pattern grow together on articulated objects) and an OakInk2 report that calls the residual within-take change 'spatial re-adjustment as much as amount'.
The table 'OakInk2-ext' column of the cross-dataset report is over all 65 extended groups (time/take amount 1.3596); the control comparison over the 39 common groups gives 1.3819.
No cross-dataset figure exists in the sources (reports/figures is empty); the page figure is built from crossdataset_exp1.csv.
entries.claim_as_extracted: Across the three datasets the within-take change of the normalised spatial pattern is near or below the take-to-take difference (time/take 1.04 TACO, 0.94 ARCTIC, 0.45 OakInk2) while an identity axis is above it (mesh 1.48 on TACO, subject 1.16 over the same-subject take level on ARCTIC, object instance 1.69 on OakInk2); whether the amount shows a temporal excess depends on how a take is cut (2.12 on TACO takes with approach and release, 1.10 on long multi-episode ARCTIC takes, 0.60 on interaction-only OakInk2 segments).
entries.correction_reason: Values confirmed. Two problems in the wording: (1) 'an identity axis is above it' puts ARCTIC's 1.16 against the take-to-take level, but its denominator is the same-subject take level; against the take level it is 1.011 (16 of 22 groups). (2) 'depends on how a take is cut' is a causal statement across datasets that differ in many other ways; the only direct evidence is the OakInk2 control, which also changes the take sample. Use 'differs in line with' and 'is consistent with'.

entries.claim: The temporal excess of the amount is associated with pairs in which at least one frame has low or zero contact: on TACO the amount time/take is 0.94 when both frames are at or above the group-median amount (4 of 8 groups above 1) but 1.44 when both frames have a vertex within 1 cm (6 of 8), and the pattern ratio is below 1 under both restrictions (0.65 and 0.80); on ARCTIC the amount ratio is 0.90 (|delta mass|) and 0.98 (log-mass) when neither frame is zero-contact. The reports read this as approach / release grading on TACO and as on/off between contact episodes on ARCTIC.
entries.metric: Macro time/take ratio (mean over pairs, phase tolerance 0.10, touching windows) recomputed on restricted pair sets: both_nonzero (neither frame zero-contact), high_contact (both frames at or above the group-median mass), both_hard (both frames have an object vertex within 1 cm of the hand). 1 = cross-take level; no direction is better.
caveats: Keep both TACO restrictions: 'the time excess disappears in firm contact' holds for the above-median restriction (0.94) and not for the 1 cm rule (1.44).
On TACO the excess is hovering-to-firm-contact grading, not on/off (at most 6.6 % of time pairs have one zero frame); on ARCTIC it is on/off (22-36 % of time pairs). The mechanisms differ by dataset.
Soft contact has a long tail (a hand hovering 4 cm away still gives about 0.13 per vertex), so 'amount' includes near-contact, not only touching.
These restricted values are from the verification table (float32 recomputation; they differ from ratios.csv in the 8th digit).
entries.claim_as_extracted: The temporal excess of the amount is associated with approach / release and on-off phases of a take: on TACO it disappears when both frames are above the group-median amount (time/take 0.94) but remains 1.44 when both frames merely have a vertex within 1 cm, and in both restrictions the pattern ratio is below 1 (0.65 and 0.80); on ARCTIC it disappears once both frames are in contact.
entries.correction_reason: Numbers confirmed in the two verify tables. Approach and release phases are not labelled on TACO or ARCTIC; the restrictions select pairs by contact amount, so 'associated with approach / release phases' is the reports' interpretation, not the measured condition. 'Disappears' for 0.94 hides that 4 of 8 groups are still above 1. ARCTIC values should be stated, and 'in contact' means 'neither frame zero-contact'.

entries.claim: Secondary (lag structure): within a take the normalised pattern does change with time lag on every dataset; at about 1 s (lag 32 frames) it reaches 0.67 of the cross-take level on TACO, 0.54 on ARCTIC and 0.25 on OakInk2, against 1.28, 0.56 and 0.32 for the amount, so the amount outruns the pattern on TACO while the two grow together on ARCTIC and OakInk2.
entries.metric: Experiment 2: mean distance between frames t and t + lag of one take (frames at 30 fps, 'touching' set = both frames non-zero, per-take means), divided by the group's matched-phase cross-take distance of the same metric; macro over groups. 1 = cross-take level. 'top-10 % share' = fraction of a take's summed frame-to-frame change carried by its 10 % largest frames, against an iid half-normal null. No direction is better.

dataset_differences: Amount, time/take (macro): TACO 2.12 (8 of 8 groups above 1), ARCTIC 1.10 (14 of 22; log-mass 1.57, 22 of 22), OakInk2 0.60 (2 of 39). 'The amount changes much more over time' is a TACO result; on ARCTIC it is weak on |delta mass| and on OakInk2 there is no temporal excess.

Pattern, time/take (macro): TACO 1.04 (3 of 8 groups above 1), ARCTIC 0.94 (6 of 22), OakInk2 0.45 (0 of 39). On TACO the within-take pattern change is about equal to the take-to-take difference, not smaller.

Identity axis differs by dataset: TACO mesh/take 1.48 (8 of 8); OakInk2 object-instance/take 1.69 (16 of 17 groups, the other 22 groups have no mesh axis); ARCTIC has one mesh per object and uses subject / SAME-SUBJECT take 1.16 (22 of 22). Against the take level used by the time ratios, ARCTIC subject/take is 1.011.
OakInk2 also has a subject axis: subject/take 1.066 on the pattern (35 of 39), measured against the any-subject take level, so it is the analogue of ARCTIC's 1.011, not of ARCTIC's 1.156.

What a take is: TACO one (verb, tool, target) recording with approach and release, 64-448 windowed frames (median 128 = 4.3 s), 2.8 % zero-contact frames; ARCTIC one recording of one articulated object, 512-1088 frames (median 704 = 23.5 s), 17 % zero-contact frames; OakInk2 the interaction range of one program primitive, 64-1856 frames (median 128), 0.16 % zero-contact frames.

Source of the temporal amount change: TACO hovering-to-firm-contact grading (0.7-6.6 % of time pairs have one zero frame; time/take amount 0.94 when both frames are above median mass, 1.44 under the 1 cm rule); ARCTIC on/off between episodes (22-36 % of time pairs; 0.90 / 0.98 once both frames are non-zero); OakInk2 none.

OakInk2 control with approach and retreat put back (39 common groups): time/take amount 0.60 to 1.38 (2 to 33 groups above 1), pattern 0.45 to 0.61 (0 to 2 groups). The control exists for OakInk2 only and for Experiments 1-2 only.

Lag structure: on TACO the amount outruns the pattern (lag 32: 1.28 vs 0.67 of the cross-take level); on ARCTIC (0.56 vs 0.54) and OakInk2 (0.32 vs 0.25) the two grow together and stay below the cross-take level within 2 s.

Group structure and size: TACO 8 groups (category x role x hand), 222-897 takes per group; ARCTIC 22 groups (object x hand), 23-30 takes per group; OakInk2 39 groups (category x hand), 20-160 takes per group, 1,985 takes analysed of 4,603 extracted.
Within-take pairs per group: TACO 3074-13369, ARCTIC 473-612, OakInk2 291-2839 (cross axes up to 4000 each), so ARCTIC per-group intervals are the widest.
Robustness checks differ: the aligned-canonicalisation rerun exists for TACO only (amount 2.27, pattern 1.03); it was not run on ARCTIC or OakInk2.
Qualitative renders exist for TACO only.
Object-trajectory predictability of the amount on held-out takes: TACO R2 0.67 / 0.70, ARCTIC 0.32 / 0.30, OakInk2 negative.
do_not_claim: 'Contact does not move over time' or 'the spatial pattern is constant within a take': the pattern changes with lag on all three datasets, exceeds the take level in 3 of 8 TACO groups and 6 of 22 ARCTIC groups, and the reports show a migrating take.
'Within a take the spatial pattern varies less than between takes' as a general statement: true on OakInk2 (0.45), marginal on ARCTIC (0.94), not true on TACO as a macro mean (1.04; pooled 0.96).
'On all datasets the amount changes much more over time than the pattern': only TACO shows it (2.12 vs 1.04); ARCTIC 1.10 vs 0.94, OakInk2 0.60 vs 0.45 with both below the take level.
That the amount ratio and the pattern ratio are directly comparable magnitudes: they are different metrics, each divided by its own cross-take level.
'Grasp identity changes the pattern': no grasp label or grasp axis exists in this study; the measured axes are take, mesh / object instance, subject and action (verb).
'Geometry changes the pattern by 1.48x' as a pure geometry effect: TACO meshes are confounded with the subjects who used them; on ARCTIC the subject axis is confounded with session and hand size.
A single 'subject/take' number comparable across ARCTIC and OakInk2: ARCTIC's 1.16 is over the same-subject take level, OakInk2's 1.07 over the any-subject take level.
'The temporal amount excess disappears in firm contact' without the second number: on TACO it is 0.94 above median mass but 1.44 under the 1 cm hard-contact rule.
Any confidence interval or significance statement for the macro ratios: the sources give bootstrap intervals per group only.
That OakInk2 was analysed on 4,603 takes: 1,985 takes entered the analysis.
That the OakInk2 control isolates the effect of approach and retreat on identical takes: the two runs contain different take samples (1,985 vs 3,239 takes in the common groups).
A pooled or averaged cross-dataset ratio: none exists in the sources and none should be computed.
That these ratios show time is 'irrelevant' or 'noise', or that a static contact map is sufficient: the ARCTIC report states that one static map per take is not enough on long articulated takes.
That this study shows a better contact representation improves hand-motion generation: the TACO report says it does not measure that.
Causal wording such as 'approach and release cause the amount change': the sources show an association through pair restrictions and one control, not an intervention on the same takes.
